Summary:
This paper tackles the problem that reinforcement-learning (RL) agents operating in safety-critical settings (e.g. autonomous driving) can catastrophically violate constraints while they are still learning. Existing “safe exploration” techniques rely on smoothness assumptions and probabilistic guarantees that often do not hold in practice, making them too conservative or simply ineffective. The authors propose a human‐teaching–inspired framework in which an automatic monitor oversees the agent. The monitor detects dangerous behaviour and activates one of several pre-defined reset controllers that drive the agent back to a safe region. A separate teacher policy learns, over time, which reset controller to apply in which circumstance (a curriculum) so as to maximise the agent’s final task reward while keeping it safe. Experiments in two simulated domains demonstrate both fewer safety violations and faster learning.

Key limitations:
• The excerpt is short; deeper implementation details (e.g. specific danger detectors) are not available, so some implementation granularity may be missing.
• Experimental evidence strength cannot be fully assessed without numerical results, therefore edge confidences are capped at 3–4.
